Title: 'Reacher' Season 4 Star Officially Breaks Down His Character's Shock Finale Decision
Article_Text:
[Editor's Note: The following contains spoilers for Reacher Season 4]
Summary
- Christopher Marquette’s Jacob Merrick is Season 4’s emotional core and breakout performance.
- He spares Amisha, choosing arrest over death—fulfilling Jacob’s hero’s journey, not a breakdown.
- The season packs nonstop twists; Jacob’s pulled through CIA plots, betrayals, and tough losses.
Prime Video’s Reacher is guaranteed to pack a punch each season, but the Alan Ritchson-led series returned with a particularly strong beating heart at its center in Season 4. After a recasting incident and an unexpected 15-minute audition, actor Christopher Rodriguez Marquette was tapped to play police officer Jacob Merrick, who Collider’s David Caballero calls “the season's emotional core” in his review of the season. Amid a powerful ensemble, one of Marquette’s most dramatic roles to date made him one of the season’s breakout performances.
In Season 4, Merrick is embroiled in the twisted conspiracy Reacher has found himself in after a woman — who turns out to be Merrick’s sister, Anna (Karen Kwong-Chip) — takes her own life on a train in Philadelphia. This tragedy only scratches the surface of a mystery involving the CIA, double-crossing allies, and a flash drive, and their investigation puts Merrick through the wringer physically and mentally.
During a conversation with Collider’s Steve Weintraub, Marquette talks spoilers, discussing Jacob’s decision to spare Amisha’s (Anggun) life, the biggest Season 4 twist that took him by surprise, and how Jacob’s hero’s journey connects to Reacher’s evolution. Don’t miss the full interview in the video above, with a transcript provided below.
Why Didn't Jacob Kill Amisha?
"I think that embodies the hero's journey."
COLLIDER: In the last episode, you elect not to kill Amisha. Talk a little bit about your reaction to that. Do you agree with Jacob's decision? Did you want Jacob to shoot? Talk about filming that.
CHRISTOPHER RODRIGUEZ MARQUETTE: I do agree with it. I think that embodies the hero's journey, right? Especially his in particular. Jacob's journey is one where you're going to see a good person access the worst parts of themselves that they didn't know existed prior to this experience and become quite volatile for a person who's not volatile, who's actually quite peaceful. So, to me, that is the right culmination and ending to a hero's journey like that. If someone breaks, they're a villain. That's the idea. So, I do agree with it.
I found it was one of the big challenges for me as an actor doing it, though, because I had to do all of that reading of the Miranda rights to arresting somebody. It's not a dialogue scene. I had to do it by way of reading the cliché, like, “You have the right to remain silent,” that whole thing, which I had never done in anything before anyway. So, it was a really cool challenge to say, “Oh yeah, I'm going to try to embody that decision and that journey and that ending in that way, through this moment of arresting somebody with Miranda rights.”
But I do agree. Yeah, I do agree. I think if it's any other way, if it's some gangster thing and he walks over and just puts a bullet in her, for me, you'd go, “Why did we care about all of this stuff that he's…?” That's the hopeful thing in the whole journey of this character — and Reacher as a whole. I sort of thought the narrative of Jacob was how Reacher becomes Reacher. Alan [Ritchson] and I talked about that, and [Nick] Santora and I talked about that. It's the embodiment: a good guy who's going to go do bad things, and where does that put you? On what side of the line are you standing on? Good versus evil. That kind of stuff. So, I think that decision is reflective of what we were exploring with all of it.
Jacob Marquette on 'Reacher' Season 4's Most Shocking Twists
"The angst, the stress, the anxiety, the trouble, the villain, it does not stop."
In general for the season, were there any other big twists or turns as you were reading the script that you were surprised by, or were you told the arc of everyone's characters?
MARQUETTE: No, I was really surprised by a few things. I was really surprised by a lot of Sampson's twists and turns. I was really surprised by his fate, and stopping the bomber and dying in the process. That was really unexpected for me.
I also really loved how Amisha and Lila’s storylines unfold and untangle. I like that it's not straight; it's not just good until wonk. It sort of goes like this for a bit. That stuff was really unexpected.
The big thing that took me by surprise was when Jacob's uncle picks him up, and you think he's finally safe, and he's not. That was really cool. I remember reading that, and I was like, “Oh, I really thought they were going to give this guy a break for a second.” I really thought he got a reprieve. So it was such cool thinking. I was like, “Right. Don't stop. This is Reacher. It doesn't stop. The angst, the stress, the anxiety, the trouble, the villain, it does not stop.” So, I love that twist as well.
Chris Marquette on Playing a Cop Who "Shouldn’t Be on This Journey"
He discusses exploring Jacob's trauma and transformation throughout Season 4.
Also, your character gets put through the wringer through the season. It's a great role on one of the most popular shows on television, so congratulations.
MARQUETTE: I really appreciate that, Steven. Thank you, man. Yeah, I feel really lucky and fortunate. I remember Nick Santora, toward the end, we were talking on the phone about the final-final scene with the funeral and releasing the ashes. He goes, “Yeah, man, so this is it. He's going to go out there, he's going to do this thing, and then he's going to go do massive amounts of therapy.” [Laughs] I was like, “Yeah, man.” This poor guy, man. This poor guy.
For real, though, he is put through the wringer. Also, as an actor, a role like this has to be gratifying because if you’re playing someone who's one-dimensional the whole season, that's hard. With this, at least you get to show so many different sides.
MARQUETTE: Totally. I appreciate that. It really was, man. I mean, it's my preference. Where I've found my usefulness as an actor has always been in sort of trying to bring some dynamic, layered performing to things. Historically, most cop shows, but definitely Reacher, who teams up with Reacher are two people, and while they're very layered, sophisticated characters always, they’re two people that are cops, and they're in already from the get-go. They're going to solve the crime. They're not necessarily going through trauma and crisis, and they're prepared for what they're doing to some degree. So, yeah, it was a really cool role to be able to play against all that, someone who actually shouldn't be on this journey and doesn't fit that mold. It gave me a lot of really interesting room to work.
Nothing was scripted where I started to find we'd be filming and Reacher would do Reacher things, and I started reacting like a normal person would. Like, at one point he gives us these burner phones and he's like, “Alright, here. I just memorized the numbers. I'm gonna call you guys in like two seconds.” It happened so quick, so every time we did it, I would just sort of shake my head and look around at everyone else, like, “Is that normal?” They’re like, “It's not normal.” And they kept a lot of these little subtle reactions throughout it, which was really nice. I was like, “That's what would happen.” All the other cops were like, “Cool. We got it. Yeah. Let's go. Let's go storm the building.” And this guy's just like, “Did you see this? The math he did was insane!” So, it was really fun to play with that, too.

Title: New laws trigger a fresh legal fight over Nazi-looted art in Los Angeles and Auschwitz museums
Article_Text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Jewish heirs of Holocaust victims and their representatives have filed two lawsuits in California staking their claims to Nazi-looted paintings that still hang on the walls of prominent museums in Los Angeles and Auschwitz.
This pair of lawsuits are the first to be filed after the recent passage of laws by California and Congress, which strengthen U.S.-based claims to artwork that were forcibly taken from Jewish families during World War II.
One lawsuit was filed in Los Angeles Superior Court on Monday by the Jewish Federation of Greater Los Angeles and its board chair Daniel Gryczman against Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena for the return of “Adam and Eve.” These are two life-size oil-on-panel masterpieces created by Lucas Carnach the Elder in 1530.
The other lawsuit was filed in federal court in Los Angeles the same day by the daughters of the late Dinah Gottliebova Babbitt, a Holocaust survivor and California-based animator who was held in Auschwitz. It demanded the return of watercolors of fellow prisoners that the artist was forced to paint for Josef Mengele, a Nazi physician who had earned the nickname the “Angel of Death.”
Spokespersons for both museums say the museums legally hold titles to the works, and intend to continue displaying them to the public. The lawsuits don’t specify the monetary value of the paintings.
Artworks pit Jewish families against museums
The issue of Nazi-looted art is an emotional, legally and ethically charged topic that pits Jewish families that have suffered inter-generational trauma against museums that say they are trying to preserve a painful, yet important, chapter of history. Between 1933 and 1945, the Nazi regime orchestrated the largest art theft in world history, seizing over 600,000 works of art across Europe from Jewish families, collectors and museums. Decades later, many of these masterpieces reside in prominent museums around the world, making the push for their recovery more complex than a simple property dispute.
Rabbi Noah Farkas is president and CEO of the Jewish Federation of Los Angeles, the organization to which Marei von Saher, sole heir of Dutch Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker, has signed over her rights. The paintings were seized from Goudstikker's collection by Hermann Goring, Adolf Hitler’s second-in-command and changed a number of hands before being sold in the 1960s to the Pasadena Museum of Modern Art, which was renamed Norton Simon Museum in honor of its benefactor.
Farkas said the federation plans to use most of the net proceeds from the recovered art to provide much-needed help to the about 2,500 Holocaust survivors living in the Los Angeles area.
“These are incredibly beautiful European masterpieces stolen from a Jewish family to enrich the Nazi party and fund the war and death machine against the people,” he said. “It's our honor to take on this role on behalf of the community and use most of the proceeds to help these elderly survivors live out the last years of their lives in dignity, comfort and peace – something their family members were denied during the Holocaust.”
Marei von Saher, in a statement, said she is grateful to the Jewish organization for taking up her family’s cause.
“This effort represents a meaningful step toward justice for Holocaust survivors and victims of Nazi era atrocities,” she said.
New legislation gives lawsuits second wind
California Assemblyman Jesse Gabriel, D-Woodland Hills, wrote Assembly Bill 2867, signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom in September 2024, which requires that the state law must apply in lawsuits brought by California residents or their heirs to recover art seized during the Holocaust or during other acts of persecution. Gabriel, who co-chairs the California Legislative Jewish Caucus, introduced the legislation in response to a federal court ruling, which allowed the state-owned Thyssen-Bornemisza National Museum in Madrid to keep a multimillion-dollar Camille Pissarro impressionist masterpiece.
That painting had been taken by the Nazis from the Cassirer family in 1939. This case, which prompted this new law, is expected to be heard in federal court in California next month.
Gabriel said it’s time for museums to “do some deep introspection on whether they want to be on the right side of history.”
Museums want to preserve paintings for posterity
Norton Simon Museum released a statement pointing out that a federal court in 2018 unanimously determined that the museum had proper title to the Cranach paintings. In May 2019, the U.S. Supreme Court declined to get involved in the case, leaving in place lower court rulings.
They said the Cranach paintings, which originally belonged to the Stroganoff family, were put up for sale in 1931 by the Soviet Union in an illicit auction in Berlin where they were purchased by Goudstikker. After a complicated journey, the paintings were sold to the museum by a Stroganoff family descendant. The museum later restored and preserved the pieces.
“For nearly 50 years, they have been on view at the Norton Simon Museum and will continue to be accessible to the public for years to come,” the statement said.
Pawel Sawicki, a spokesperson for the Auschwitz Memorial, said the watercolors of Roma victims that Gottliebova Babbitt was forced to paint by Mengele to document his horrendous experiments and racial research, “must remain in the Memorial” to document the man's crimes. He said these paintings must not be mischaracterized as “Nazi-looted art” because Gottliebova Babbitt painted them against her will as a prisoner and therefore didn’t have ownership of the watercolors.
While he understands the family’s sentiments, Sawicki said the portraits of Roma and Sinti victims are among the few remaining documents of Mengele’s criminal experiments and should be treated as unique documents related to the history of the Auschwitz concentration camp.
“While fully respecting the rights of people who created some of the documents here, we are of the opinion that any loss in the collections of the Memorial will constitute irreparable harm,” he said. “ … The loss of even the smallest part of the documentation is an irreparable loss and blemish on the memory of the victims of Auschwitz.”
Advocates hope cases will now be heard on their merit
Joel Greenberg, founder of Art Ashes, a Philadelphia-area nonprofit that helps Jewish families track down and recover Nazi-looted art, said in addition to the California law, President Donald Trump signed into law and updated the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2025. This new law permanently eliminated the expiration date to allow Holocaust survivors and their heirs to indefinitely pursue the recovery of these works of art.
Greenberg said the new federal law gave families the right to reclaim their art for up to six years from the time they find out in whose possession they are.
“These new laws mean that technical defenses will no longer stick in court,” he said. “Every case will be heard on its merits.”
He said the new legislation also ensures that these Jewish families have their day in court and a fair process to determine ownership of the stolen art.
“It will make sure the stories of what happened to European Jewry is not lost and forgotten,” he said. “The art can still be returned to the rightful owner.”

Title: Illegal Alien Pleads Guilty in Grandparent Scam Money Laundering Case, Faces Up to 20 Years
Article_Text:
A Dominican Republic resident illegally living in Perth Amboy, New Jersey, pleaded guilty in federal court to a charge of money laundering conspiracy in connection with a grandparent fraud scheme, United States Attorney Troy Rivetti announced today.
Elvys Nicanor Nunez Valerio, 33, pleaded guilty to one count before Senior United States District Judge Nora Barry Fischer on September 14, 2026.
In connection with the guilty plea, the Court was advised that Valerio was a participant in a sophisticated grandparent fraud scheme operating out of the Dominican Republic in which an organized crime group impersonating a grandchild — or other close relative — in a crisis contacted elderly victims and asked for immediate financial assistance. The scammers arranged for a rideshare driver to pick up cash from the elderly relative and deliver the money to a member of the criminal group. From there, portions of the money were deposited into bank accounts or sent back to the Dominican Republic via money transfer services. Specifically, Valerio’s role in the conspiracy was to receive the fraud proceeds from the rideshare drivers, to further launder the money, and ultimately to transfer the money to the Dominican Republic.
On July 12, 2025, an elderly resident of the Western District of Pennsylvania was contacted as part of the grandparent scheme and was deceived into providing $10,000 to a rideshare driver who came to his home to pick up the funds. Subsequently, the victim's family learned of the fraud and contacted the Pennsylvania State Police. The victim was still in contact with the scammer, who instructed the victim to pay another $12,000 so that his daughter could be released from prison. A driver picked up the second package, which did not contain any fraud proceeds. The Pennsylvania State Police initiated a traffic stop on the rideshare driver, who was an unknowing participant in the fraud. Authorities then allowed the driver to deliver the package to its destination address in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. The driver provided the second package to Valerio, who was stopped by the Pennsylvania State Police before he was able to drive away.
A search of the vehicle resulted in the recovery of the second package as well as fraud proceeds associated with the first package. Further investigation revealed that Valerio was involved in the larger conspiracy and had traveled around the country participating in the fraud. Activity in a bank account in Valerio’s name was determined to be consistent with involvement in the scheme, including, between January and July 2025, more than 40 cash deposits totaling more than $65,000. The financial records also showed payments to and from other members of the conspiracy and transfers of the fraud proceeds to the Dominican Republic.
Judge Fischer scheduled sentencing for December 1, 2026. The law provides for a total sentence of up to 20 years in prison, a fine of up to $500,000, or both. Under the federal Sentencing Guidelines, the actual sentence imposed is based upon the seriousness of the offense and the prior criminal history, if any, of the defendant.
Two of Valerio’s co-conspirators, Luis Alfonso Bisono Rodriguez and Engels Guillermo Almengot Valerio, both also of the Dominican Republic and illegally residing in the U.S., each were sentenced by Judge Fischer earlier this month to two years of prison, to be followed by three years of supervised release, on their convictions for money laundering conspiracy in relation to the grandparent fraud scheme.
Assistant United States Attorney Brendan T. Conway is prosecuting this case on behalf of the government.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation and Pennsylvania State Police, in conjunction with numerous other police departments throughout the United States, conducted the investigation that led to the prosecution of Valerio.

Title: Saturday Sports Headlines and Scores presented by Barton Community College
Article_Text:
Lane Kiffin was wildly booed long before he arrived at Vaught-Hemingway Stadium for the LSU-Ole Miss game. Kiffin appeared remotely on ESPN’s “College GameDay,” and Mississippi fans still angry about how he left Oxford for Baton Rouge late last season greeted him with a chorus of expletive-laced chants. It was a clear sign of what Kiffin and the Tigers should expect when they play at Ole Miss later Saturday. Kiffin says: “I really appreciate you guys gaslighting them with this." It was the latest in a growing buildup for the first top-10 matchup between No. 7 LSU and eight-ranked Ole Miss since 1962.
HOUSTON (AP) — The Atlanta Braves are back in the playoffs after missing out last season. The first-place Braves beat the Houston Astros 6-2 to punch their ticket to the postseason for the eighth time in nine years. They clinched at least a National League wild card and reduced their magic number to three for winning the NL East. Michael Harris II, Ronald Acuña Jr. and Matt Olson each hit a two-run homer for the Braves. Atlanta is trying to hold off the Philadelphia Phillies for the NL East title and could wrap up the division crown as soon as Sunday. Atlanta’s win Friday night coupled with Philadelphia’s 6-3 loss to the Mets gave the Braves a five-game lead over the Phillies with eight to play.
Arsenal slumped to a first loss of its Premier League title defense and it was a heavy one at Brighton. The champions' 3-0 defeat at Amex Stadium came somewhat out of nowhere after four straight wins. Conceding the third goal from a corner — typically an area of strength for Arsenal — summed up an unusually sloppy performance from Mikel Arteta’s team. Pascal Gross and Charalampos Kostoulas scored in the first half with shots from outside the penalty area, before Chema Andres completed the win with a header at the back post from Gross’ corner. Big-spending Tottenham is still without a win this season after losing 3-2 against Aston Villa. Newcastle and Everton also won.
WINSTON-SALEM, N.C. (AP) — Darian Mensah connected on his first 24 passes on the way to setting Atlantic Coast Conference records for consecutive completions, and fifth-ranked Miami’s defense came up with four straight fourth-quarter stops to beat Wake Forest 33-20 on Friday night. Mensah completed 30 of 34 passes for 220 yards and three touchdowns. He helped the Hurricanes take a 31-7 lead midway through the third quarter. The defense stepped up when the offense slowed, including a late interception. Gio Lopez threw for 312 yards and three touchdowns to lead Wake Forest.
NAGOYA, Japan (AP) — The opening ceremony of the Asian Games has marked the official start of the 16-day event. But Saturday's official opening was not really the beginning. Facing a packed schedule, competition in basketball started on September 10. The semifinals in men’s basketball were on Friday. Soccer has been going on for almost as long. The Summer Olympics typically start a few days early, but this multi-sport event pushes the envelope. The Asian Games feature at least 11,000 athletes. The 2024 Summer Olympics had 10,700. The last Asian Games in Hangzhou, China, in 2023 had about 12,000 athletes and this could match it.
LUBBOCK, Texas (AP) — J’Koby Williams and Cameron Dickey ran for second-half touchdowns and defending Big 12 champion No. 13 Texas Tech held on for a 28-26 win when Houston quarterback Conner Weigman came up just short of a 2-point conversion in the final minute. Weigman’s third TD pass, a 10-yarder to Patrick Overmyer with 49 seconds left, gave the 2-1 Cougars a chance to tie in the conference opener for both teams Friday night. On the try for 2, Weigman took off to the left and lunged forward with the ball extended, though his knee came down before the ball broke the plane of the end zone. Will Hammond was 17-of-27 passing for 257 yards and a touchdown for the 3-0 Red Raiders.
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Aaron Donald expects to play for the Los Angeles Rams in their home opener against the New York Giants on Monday night. Donald, a three-time Associated Press Defensive Player of the Year and eight-time All-Pro defensive lineman, had been out of football for the previous two seasons before ending his retirement in August. He did not travel with the Rams for their season opener in Melbourne, Australia, and instead remained in Southern California to continue preparations.
Alexander Zverev gives Germany a 1-0 lead over Croatia in the last qualifying round for the Davis Cup Final 8 by beating Matej Dodig 6-4, 7-6 (3). It was Zverev’s first match since winning the U.S. Open last weekend. That came after the 29-year-old Zverev won his first Grand Slam title at the French Open in June. The second-ranked Zverev had 15 aces and dominated on the indoor hardcourt in Halle, Germany, with Dodig having no break-point chances. American pair Christian Harrison and Austin Krajicek made it 2-1 against the Czech Republic after winning in doubles. Shelton will have a chance to seal the series in Prague if he can beat Jakub Mensik a day after he lost to Jiri Lehecka and allowed the Czechs level the score at 1-1.
TORONTO (AP) — Kelsey Mitchell walked into a postgame celebration without realizing she was the guest of honor. Mitchell scored 33 points to set a WNBA season scoring record in Friday’s 103-85 win over the Toronto Tempo. With a 3-pointer in the third quarter, Mitchell eclipsed the 1,021 points A’ja Wilson scored for Las Vegas in 2024. Mitchell has scored 1,034 points this season. Mitchell also scored at least 20 points for the 25th consecutive game, extending her WNBA record. She shot 12 for 17 and went 7 for 11 from 3-point range.
PHOENIX (AP) — Three-time AL MVP Aaron Judge will miss most or all of the rest of the regular season after the New York Yankees announced they are placing him on the 10-day injured list because of a right calf strain. New York said it will make the roster move on Saturday. The placement could be backdated to Thursday, meaning it is possible Judge could return for New York’s regular-season finale on Sept. 27. Title: Torrid Padres take on Marlins, hoping to keep pace in NL wild-card race
Article_Text:
Field Level Media
                
19 Sep 2026, 20:10 GMT+10
            
(Photo credit: David Frerker)
Friday night couldn't have gone any better for the San Diego Padres.
Not only did they continue their scalding September with an 8-2 defeat of the visiting Miami Marlins, but losses by the Chicago Cubs and Philadelphia enabled the Padres (85-69) to forge a three-way tie atop the National League wild-card standings. And their magic number to clinch a playoff spot was reduced to four when the New York Yankees defeated Arizona.
San Diego will hope for similar results on Saturday when it looks to improve to 5-0 this season against Miami.
The Padres are presently flying on a rocket ship to the postseason. They've won 11 of their last 12 games and have scored at least six runs in seven of their last eight. The idea of actually hosting a wild-card series is now taking on serious traction.
While San Diego would lose any tiebreaker with the Phillies or Cubs, it is easily the hottest of the three clubs coming down the home stretch.
'The only thing that we can worry about is playing each game the best we can and playing to our standard,' said manager Craig Stammen. 'That first playoff game, we would love for it to be in San Diego.'
The Padres are 47-29 in Petco Park, including a 22-5 mark dating back to July 10. The only home series they've lost since late June came at Pittsburgh's hands in late August.
'We're in a good spot going into these last eight games,' said first baseman Ty France, who belted his career-high 21st homer to cap a six-run fifth inning Friday night. 'Hopefully, we can just keep things going.'
Casey Mize (6-9, 3.69 ERA) will try to string together consecutive wins for San Diego. He scattered eight hits over five innings Monday night in an 8-7 victory at Colorado, allowing two runs. He is 1-1 with a 2.31 ERA in two prior starts against Miami.
Eury Perez (7-11, 3.99) looks to escape the roughest patch of his season, one that's seen him allow 19 earned runs in his last four starts, covering 16 2/3 innings. The best start in that stretch came Sunday in a 6-4 win over the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Perez made it through five innings, allowing four hits and three runs with two walks and five strikeouts. Control has been an issue as he's doled out 12 walks in that span. He's 0-1 with a 3.75 ERA in two career outings against San Diego.
The loss came on July 25, when he worked seven innings and yielded three runs in an eventual 7-2 defeat that was the 11th game in a 12-game losing streak that eventually took Miami (76-78) out of the running.
With Miami out of the playoffs for a third straight season, it will use the remaining time to try to find answers for an inconsistent bullpen. Season-ending injuries to closer Pete Fairbanks and setup man Anthony Bender have made things harder.
Manager Clayton McCullough said he won't have a set closer over the final eight games.
'We just look at using the best people we have to get to that point and then whoever's left will get that opportunity,' he said.
--Field Level Media

Title: Yanks move on without Aaron Judge as D-backs fight to stay alive
Article_Text:
Field Level Media
                
19 Sep 2026, 19:49 GMT+10
            
(Photo credit: Kirby Lee)
The New York Yankees will play the rest of the regular season without slugger Aaron Judge. While they understand the magnitude of his loss, they enter the stretch run with belief.
The Yanks scored five runs in the first inning of a 9-2 victory over the Arizona Diamondbacks in the first game of a weekend series Friday, and the teams meet again Saturday in Phoenix as Arizona attempts to stay alive in the National League wild-card race.
'Obviously losing 'Judgey' hurts,' Cody Bellinger said. 'We all know he's the best hitter in the game. For us in here, our mindset is we're going to have to find a way. The talent in this room speaks for itself.
'I'm fully confident we have enough talent in here that we can go out and win and beat anybody.'
American League Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.95 ERA) will face Arizona right-hander Brandon Pfaadt (7-3, 3.77) in the second game of the series.
The Diamondbacks (80-74) will ask Pfaadt to end a slump in which they have lost five of six. They are five games behind San Diego, the Chicago Cubs and Philadelphia (all 85-69) for the three NL wild-card spots with eight games to play.
'We know where we're at,' Arizona manager Torey Lovullo said. 'We can't afford to worry about things we can't control. I'm going to say there's time. There's always time.'
The Yankees (89-64) are 48-39 this season without Judge, who was placed on the injured list Friday with a strained right calf after missing three months earlier with a fractured right rib.
New York is also without injured regulars Jazz Chisholm Jr. (thumb) and Trent Grisham (hamstring), although manager Aaron Boone said Chisholm could return for the Tampa Bay series early next week.
The Yankees, who already have qualified for the postseason, are four games behind Tampa Bay in the AL East, and the teams have a four-game series at Yankee Stadium beginning Tuesday.
'There is no replacing a player as great as Aaron Judge, but we have high expectations that don't change now,' Boone said. 'One thing we do know is that we are in the dance.
'We've been built on the strength of our starting pitching all year.'
No one has been as strong as Schlittler, who is in his first full season and has made every start while Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodon have missed time with injuries or recovery time.
Schlittler has won four of his last five starts and has given up one run or fewer in each of his last seven. He was struck on the back of his right leg by Bo Bichette's 111.5 mph comebacker on his 94th and last pitch of a 2-0 victory over the New York Mets last Sunday, but shrugged it off.
'You have an ace at the top that has pitched like that,' Boone said. 'That's a good place to start. He's been dominant. This is largely in line with who we saw down the stretch last year.'
Schlittler has never faced the Diamondbacks, although Jesus Sanchez is 4 for 12 with three walks against him.
Pfaadt is 0-2 with a 5.74 ERA in his last five starts, and he gave up six runs and 10 hits in 6 2/3 innings in a loss to Texas on Aug. 12. He will be pitching on six days' rest after being pushed back so Eduardo Rodriguez could start the first game of the series.
Pfaadt lost his only outing against the Yankees, giving up six runs in 4 1/3 innings of a 7-1 loss as a rookie in 2023. Cody Bellinger is 2 for 7 with two solo homers against him and Luis Garcia Jr. is 3 for 7 with a homer.
--Field Level Media
