Title: Lancaster Capital Day festival to move through 350 years with music, food, history
Article_Text:
Downtown Lancaster has become known for its festivals — celebrating culture, food, music and art.
On Saturday, downtown will play host to a new festival in which Lancaster celebrates itself — stemming from one special day in its long history, to be exact.
The day before the 249th anniversary of the day Lancaster became one of only nine American cities to serve as the nation’s capital, a new Lancaster Capital Day festival will take over the center of town — on the first blocks of West King and North Queen streets — with music and dance performances, food, history trivia, history tours, speakers, a historical-costume parade, craft vendors and more.
The festival, which is free to visitors, runs from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.
“It’s a showcase of Lancaster history and culture. And a lot of that is presented through the arts,” says Tim Austin, an architect with Colab XYZ in Lititz, who chairs the three-person committee of the nonprofit Keystone Events Project that is organizing Capital Day.
(The Keystone Events Project organized its fifth L’Italia festival in Lititz last weekend.)
Capital Day will be “a cultural festival with a number of food vendors, craft vendors, performances, walking tours and activities throughout the day,” Austin says.
He says the festival is a collaborative effort among many local nonprofits, businesses and volunteers.
Performances and speeches from government officials and representatives of local organizations will be presented on two downtown stages throughout the day, he says.
The main stage will be “right at the center of Penn Square, right on the footprint of the first Lancaster courthouse.” That’s where members of the Continental Congress met Sept. 27, 1777, after they fled Philadelphia as British troops occupied the city.
The second stage will be located at the Fulton Bank terrace, in front of the former Isaac’s restaurant, Austin notes.
Musical entertainment will include the Moonlighters Big Band, the Malta Band, the Barkley Cove string band, Big Boy Brass, McCaskey High School’s Drumline and more.
There will also be a spoken-word performance from Sir Dominique Jordan.
Christina McSherry, executive director of Historic Rock Ford, says the Rock Ford dance group — which presents dances from late 18th and early 19th centuries — will also perform.
Reenactors portraying historical figures of the time will be at Capital Day to interact with festivalgoers.
There will be lots of activities for children in Capital Day’s “kids zone,” including blocks they can play with and a tricorn hat decoration stand.
Austin says the Capital Day committee is also having a miniature model of the original Lancaster Courthouse built, to stand in the children’s activity area.
Central Market will have extended hours Saturday — from 6 a.m. to 5 p.m. — and a beer garden will be set up in the Hager parking lot
Moving through history
“It was important for us that we didn’t get stuck in the past,” Austin says. “It’s not just a Colonial dress-up party.”
“We (will) actually kind of look back through the centuries at, at different moments in Lancaster’s history,” Austin says, and “look at Lancaster from different angles and from different time periods.
“We have a seven-hour festival from 10 a.m. till 5 p.m. And if you move 50 years per hour, you can cover 350 years,” he says. “So we’ve established this timeline from 1681 till 2026,” from the signing of William Penn’s charter for Pennsylvania, up to the present moment.
Various historical organizations will be involved to provide information on the Civil War era, Abraham Lincoln’s funerary procession that came through Lancaster, the civil rights movement and John F. Kennedy’s 1960 presidential campaign stop in the city.
There will be a performance from Bethel AME Church’s “Living the Experience” reenactment group that will deal with the Underground Railroad and an enslaved person in Gen. Edward Hand’s home — now Historic Rock Ford — Austin says.
A speaker from Mennonite Life will talk about life in the county, outside Lancaster city.
The Latino community will be highlighted as well, Austin says, including through Latin dance lessons for the crowd with Mambojaz Studio.
The final speaker for the day will be Lancaster’s Mayor Jaime Arroyo, says Kristen Simon, bureau chief of tourism for Lancaster City.
“I think he has a compelling personal story and the timing of it is such that he can speak about Lancaster today that we know and love, and the Lancaster that he envisions for the future,” Austin says.
The city has been helping connect local organizations with the Capital Day committee since last winter, and has been doing some of the marketing for the festival, Simon says.
“We’re hoping (Capital Day) is a popular event, is well attended and that it sparks traffic to our small-business community here,” Simon says. “We have a lot of pride, right, in our city. So this is just another reason to bring our community together to celebrate. ... Hopefully this is the start of a really cool new tradition.”
A cool autumn morning
With the Battle of Brandywine lost and the British heading for Philadelphia, members of the Second Continental Congress followed their prepared plan to flee to Lancaster.
They ensconced themselves in the first Lancaster Courthouse on Sept. 27, 1777, and did a bit of business.
Still not feeling safe, they moved moved west, crossing the Susquehanna River and setting up shop in York for nine months.
With the British occupying Philadelphia, “hundreds of people are fleeing to Lancaster,” says Adam Zurn, a local historian who recently published a book about Capital Day that he’ll sell at the festival (see related story). “And, you know, they’re filling the hotels and the taverns. And people are camping on farmlands and just wherever they can find a space.
“And so when Congress gets there, there just really isn’t space for these guys to even stay long term,” Zurn says.
“John Hancock, he bangs his gavel twice at 10 a.m. on that cool autumn morning” in Lancaster, Zurn says. “And he brings a total of 28 men to order.
“And in that moment, Lancaster becomes the third capital of the United States,” Zurn says, after Philadelphia and, briefly, Baltimore.
The cities that have been the nation’s capital “is an incredibly exclusive club,” Zurn says. “There’s only nine members. And there will only ever be nine members. ... And I think it’s really cool that we’re having a one-day festival to honor that.”
“It’s, for me, like a jumping off point to really just celebrate lots of things about the city that we love and not just the history,” says Matt Johnson, who has led a movement for Capital Day recognition in Lancaster over the past 10 years.
Johnson recalls going to then-Mayor Rick Gray’s home years ago with several friends along with a signed petition and a song he had written, asking for Capital Day recognition.
“(Gray) says, by the power vested in me, by the third-class city code, I pronounce this Capital Day,” Johnson remembers. City Council eventually recognized the holiday with an official resolution, he adds.
Johnson, who is a strategic community partnerships officer with Church World Service, also got to talk about Capital Day when he was a contestant on “Jeopardy!” in 2012. Having talked about Sept. 27, 1777, in a pre-show interview, Johnson was prompted by then-host Alex Trebek to explain on the game show about Lancaster’s capital distinction.
Johnson is scheduled to talk about Capital Day and perform his Capital Day song — “based on a drinking song from a National Bohemian [beer] advertisement from the ’60s” — during Saturday’s festival.
Rock Ford’s McSherry notes that, when Gen. Edward Hand was burgess — basically the mayor — of Lancaster, he wrote to Congress in 1789, suggesting Lancaster be made the nation’s capital, permanently.
“And in that letter, he details all the reasons why Lancaster would be a fantastic capital for the entire United States,” McSherry says, making three main points about the city.
Those points are still valid ways to talk about Lancaster today, she says: Lancaster is welcoming to all kinds of people, it’s located near other major Eastern cities and it has manufacturing, agriculture and craftspeople.
McSherry hopes Capital Day will help Lancaster understand its past.
“There’s a lot of, I think, misunderstandings about what Lancaster looked like in the 18th century,” McSherry says. “I think there’s this sense that we’re this frontier town that doesn’t have a lot of infrastructure. ... And one of the things we like to talk about at Rock Ford is we were the center of craftsmanship, of manufacturing, of agriculture.
“It was a colorful town,” she adds, filled with people of different races and ethnicities, speaking different languages.
Funding for this year ... and beyond
Though putting together a festival this size will be costly, Austin says “our nonprofit has a business model that we’re actually able to, to generate some revenue ourselves” for both L’Italia and Capital Day festivals.
“Our budgets end up being about a third covered by the vendors fees themselves, a third from our sponsors,” Austin says, “and then we’re able to generate about a third of our revenue from direct sales.”
On Sunday, Sept. 27 — Capital Day itself — there will be a gala at the Hamilton Club, Austin says. “That helps us raise money, really to invest in next year, is the thinking.
“We are very hopeful that (Capital Day) becomes an annual tradition and even a holiday for the community to celebrate together,” Austin says. “Next year is an opportunity to really go big” for the 250th anniversary of Sept. 27, 1777.
”So big picture is, this is a cultural festival where we celebrate this place, Lancaster,” Austin says, “that we all call home, where we live, where we love to visit, where we have family.”

Title: This swing state Republican keeps distancing himself from Trump. It may not save him in the midterms
Article_Text:
YARDLEY, Pa. (AP) — Mary Ryan may be a registered Republican but she has never voted for President Donald Trump, turned off by his crass style of politics and chaotic approach to governing.
But the 60-year-old medical writer from the Philadelphia suburbs has consistently backed her party's congressman, five-term Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick.
Until now.
This year, Ryan is so fed up with Trump and his grip on Congress that she is planning to vote in November for Fitzpatrick's Democratic opponent in the 1st Congressional District, Bob Harvie, a twice countywide elected commissioner who is a former social studies teacher.
Even though Fitzpatrick has pitched himself as a voice of reason in Washington, Ryan said that “I don't see it happening.”
Defections like this one could sink Fitzpatrick’s reelection chances and cost Republicans their narrow U.S. House majority. As one of the few Republicans representing a congressional district won by Democrat Kamala Harris in the presidential race two years ago, Fitzpatrick has done as much as any House Republican to distance himself from Trump: Fitzpatrick voted against Trump's tariffs, his signature tax legislation and his power to wage war against Iran without congressional approval. The lawmaker even skipped Trump’s recent midterm convention in Dallas.
But that may not be enough to overcome the collateral damage of the president’s sagging approval rating and soaring fuel prices because of the war.
Fitzpatrick, speaking briefly after a Sept. 11 memorial in his district, said he understands this year's political challenges and always considers what is best for his constituents with every vote.
“That’s the job,” he said. Representatives for Fitzpatrick did not respond to requests for a more complete interview.
Democrats have tried for years to defeat Fitzpatrick
Harvie describes the race and his decision to run in almost existential terms.
“The lack of trust in our government, the lack of trust in each other and seeing each other as enemies based just on, you know, the color of your skin, the religion you practice, who you voted for,” he said in an interview this summer. “I worry about just the basic foundations of this nation.”
Fitzpatrick has consistently survived challenges in his politically mixed district. He won by 13 percentage points in 2024 when Harris won by less than a single point in the district. In 2022, he won by about 10 points when Democrats were elected to the U.S. Senate and governorship. In 2020, Democratic presidential nominee Joe Biden won the district by about 5 points while Fitzpatrick carried it by about 13 points.
“Every two years Democrats in Washington label Congressman Fitzpatrick as vulnerable. Every two years he wins anyway,” said Robert Speel, an associate professor of political science at the Penn State campus in Erie. “It’s, to some extent, possibly like Charlie Brown trying to kick the football and failing each time.”
Harvie pointed to his deep roots in the district as a basis for why he could be different from previous Democrats who ran against Fitzpatrick.
“I’m not somebody who needs to be reintroduced or introduced to people of this district. And that’s very, very different than any race he’s ever run before,” he said.
Jean Dolan, 61, is a Democratic voter from Newtown who has never backed Fitzpatrick and does not plan to this year. She has been frustrated with Trump's immigration crackdown and she worries about how anti-vaccine sentiment in his administration could affect public health. As she sees it, Fitzpatrick is not independent enough from his party's leaders.
“He's a nice guy. I know people like him a lot in the community,” she said. But, she added, “you have to serve everyone in your district."
Fitzpatrick has been willing to criticize Trump
Fitzpatrick graduated with an MBA and a law degree and worked as a special agent for the FBI and as an assistant U.S. attorney. He also worked in private practice as a lawyer and accountant before running for the seat previously held by his brother, Mike Fitzpatrick, who died of cancer in 2020.
Jim Rachau, a 45-year-old photographer from Doylestown, is a registered independent who plans to vote for Fitzpatrick again this year. Rachau is not thrilled with the war or the economy, but said Fitzpatrick has earned his support with his prior public service as an FBI agent.
“You would think serving for the public good, he would have their best interest at heart,” Rachau said.
In Congress, Fitzpatrick has not shied away from disagreeing with Trump. He criticized the president, for example, in April when Trump called Pope Leo XIV “weak,” and captive to the “Radical Left."
“There’s so many angry voices out there. We all know that's the case,” Fitzpatrick said in an episode of a podcast launched this year with U.S. Rep. Tom Suozzi, a Democrat who represents a battleground district in New York. “People are sick and tired of the noise. They’re sick and tired of elected officials not being focused on the kitchen table issues that people really care about.”
Fitzpatrick also posts online regularly about meeting with groups across the district. He recently showed up to a picket line with striking sheet metal workers; he dropped by a local Catholic church's parish picnic; and he stopped at a community college hosting a maternity coalition.
Fitzpatrick spends millions on attack ads against Harvie
Fitzpatrick has also unleashed a wave of spending in the race already, disbursing nearly $5 million, according to Federal Election Commission records.
Negative attack ads against Harvie have mushroomed. Many claim Harvie is under FBI investigation, which the Democrat denies. He has filed a federal defamation lawsuit against a super PAC running some of the ads.
According to the suit, local media reported in 2020 with few details that the FBI was investigating local government and that Harvie was called to testify as a witness in the case. His attorneys say he has never been charged.
The FBI did not respond to a request for comment.
No debate has been scheduled between Fitzpatrick and Harvie, but the men appeared at the same Sept. 11 memorial, standing on opposite sides of the speaker’s lectern. They did not appear to speak to each other.
Ryan, the medical writer from the Philadelphia suburbs, said she is thinking less about Fitzpatrick and more about how Republicans in Congress and their reluctance to buck the president.
“Incumbents just feel they can’t cross that line. If they do, they’re not going to get reelected," she said. But she acknowledged that may not matter in the end. "They might not get reelected anyway.”

Title: Stats that will matter in the 2026 postseason
Article_Text:
Every playoff team has its strengths, its weaknesses, its signature skills. We want to find some of the things that will matter most this October.
So we're diving into the Statcast data for the teams that are sitting in clear playoff position and picking out some of the most interesting nuggets.
Here are nine stats that could loom large this postseason.
1) The Braves have a ton of bat speed
Bat speed matters, and the Braves have a ton of it across their roster. That will surely come in handy in the postseason, when they're trying to do damage against pitches that are faster and nastier than ones they saw all year.
Atlanta is tied with the Padres and Cardinals for the highest overall bat speed of any National League team this season. And they have the highest "fast swing rate," which is how often they post bat speeds of 75 mph or faster. Over a third of the Braves' swings are fast swings -- and fast swings can simply hit the baseball harder and send it farther.
Basically every key Atlanta hitter has strong bat speed:
- Ronald Acuña Jr.: 75.8 mph
- Austin Riley: 75.8 mph
- Drake Baldwin: 75.4 mph
- Michael Harris II: 74.9 mph
- Matt Olson: 74.8 mph
All five of those hitters have fast swing rates over 50%.
2) The Rays have two stars who are polar opposites
Two of the most important players for the Rays in the playoffs will be Junior Caminero and Chandler Simpson. And they couldn't be more different as hitters.
Caminero is one of the best power hitters in the league:
- He's one of five hitters with 60-plus barrels this season -- those are balls hit with the ideal exit velocity and launch angle to turn into home runs and extra-base hits.
- He has the fastest swing in the Major Leagues, with an average bat speed of 79.6 mph. The faster your bat, the harder and farther you can hit the ball.
- Of his AL-best 41 home runs, 27 are "no-doubters" -- gone at 30/30 MLB ballparks -- the most of any slugger in the big leagues.
Simpson is ALL contact:
- He has zero barrels -- the literal only player, out of 245 qualifying hitters on Statcast's exit velocity leaderboard, without a single barrel all year.
- His bat speed, at 65.0 mph, is one of the lowest in the league.
- But with his great bat control, he squares up the ball on the sweet spot of the bat at one of the highest rates in the league, which is why he's batting .311 and might win the AL batting title.
- He ranks in the top 1% of Major League hitters in both swing-and-miss rate (just 10.4%) and strikeout rate (just 7.9%).
Home runs matter a lot in October, but so does having different types of hitters in your lineup. The Rays can beat you with a bloop or a blast.
3) The Cubs are the best fielding team of the last decade
In the playoffs, where outs are at a premium, it sure helps to have an elite defense like the Cubs.
And the 2026 Cubs' advantage in the field is like none we've seen since Statcast started tracking. They've now prevented more runs with their defense than any team of the last 10 years.
Highest team Fielding Run Value, Statcast era
- 2026 Cubs: +68 runs prevented
- 2018 D-backs: +64 runs prevented
- 2022 Yankees: +58 runs prevented
- 2019 Guardians: +58 runs prevented
- 2022 Astros: +52 runs prevented
- 2019 D-backs: +52 runs prevented
- 2024 Blue Jays: +50 runs prevented
Obviously the fulcrum of that all-world defense is Pete Crow-Armstrong in center field. PCA, on his own, is having the best individual outfield season of the Statcast era, and a top-five fielding season overall.
Top individual seasons by Fielding Run Value, Statcast era
- 2025 Patrick Bailey (catcher): +31 runs prevented
- 2018 Nick Ahmed (shortstop): +28 runs prevented
- 2026 Pete Crow-Armstrong (center field): +27 runs prevented
- 2019 Javier Báez (shortstop): +26 runs prevented
- 2017 Byron Buxton (center field): +24 runs prevented
- 2016 Adam Eaton (right field): +24 runs prevented
But it's not just PCA. Almost every Cubs fielder who plays significant innings, from Crow-Armstrong and Dansby Swanson on down, is a strong defender.
And since the Cubs pitching staff has the least velocity in the Majors, and pitchers that are both fly-ball (Shota Imanaga) and ground-ball (Clay Holmes) specialists, it's extra important to have a defense that converts all kinds of batted balls into outs.
4) Tarik Skubal's changeup is a monster in October
This is why the Dodgers got Skubal. All eyes are going to be on the back-to-back reigning Cy Young winner in the playoffs, and he might have the single best wipeout pitch of anyone in the postseason.
Skubal's changeup has been one of the best secondary pitches in baseball over the past three seasons, and it somehow gets even nastier in the playoffs.
Over his last two playoff runs with the Tigers, Skubal racked up 27 strikeouts on changeups alone -- the most by any pitcher on any one pitch type over the last two postseasons. Over half the plate appearances decided by his changeup were K's.
Most K's on one pitch type, 2024-25 postseasons
1. Tarik Skubal's changeup: 27
2. Trey Yesavage's splitter: 22 
3. Kevin Gausman's splitter: 21 
4. Tarik Skubal's 4-seamer: 19 
5-T. Carlos Rodón's slider: 18 
5-T. Blake Treinen's sweeper: 18
And the swing-and-miss rate against Skubal's changeup in the postseason? A ridiculous 71%. That's the highest for any pitch type with at least 25 swings against it from 2024-25.
5) Jacob Misiorowski's fastball is going to be a monster in October
The Miz's triple-digit heater is going to take center stage as soon as the Brewers' postseason run begins. He's spent the regular season shattering basically every velocity record we have for starting pitchers.
But what if he has even more in the tank when everything is on the line?
In the regular season, two out of every three fastballs Misiorowski throws are 100 mph or faster. Over 40% are 101 mph or faster. Over 20% are 102 mph or faster. Almost 10% are 103 mph or faster.
That is just a preposterous amount of velo when you're throwing well over 1,000 heaters over the course of a season. No starter touches the Miz there. Now what will happen in the playoffs, when there are only a few games left to pitch?
Last postseason, Misiorowski's velo got a bump from 99.3 mph to 101 mph -- albeit as he moved into a relief role -- and over three quarters of his fastballs were in triple digits. Now he's been sitting at 100.6 mph in the regular season. What if he can take it even higher …
6) Adley's defense can be a game-changer even if he's not hitting
Adley Rutschman was a blockbuster acquisition for the Red Sox at the Trade Deadline. As the Sox draw closer to the playoffs, the All-Star catcher has yet to really find his swing. But Adley can impact a playoff game just as much behind the plate as he can at the plate.
Rutschman has been one of the most valuable defensive catchers in the Majors this season, and the most valuable catcher on a team currently in playoff position. He's a great pitch framer, he controls the run game, and he's a solid blocker.
Best defensive catchers on 2026 teams in playoff position
- Adley Rutschman (Red Sox): +12 runs saved
- Freddy Fermin (Padres): +10 runs saved
- Austin Wells (Yankees): +7 runs saved
- Patrick Bailey (Guardians): +6 runs saved
- Christian Vázquez (Astros): +3 runs saved
He's also great at a new catching skill that might be magnified in the postseason: ABS challenges.
Rutschman is a very good challenger as a catcher, successfully overturning two thirds of the ball and strike calls he's challenged this season. He's 41-21 on challenges, including 19-9 since joining the Red Sox. Maybe he can create a strikeout for Boston's pitchers in a key moment or two this October.
7) The Phillies' big bashers are two of the best fastball hitters in the game
The playoffs are a showcase of the nastiest pitches in the game, and a lot of that is breaking and offspeed stuff. You have to be able to jump on fastballs when you get them -- even if they're the overpowering, extra-high-velocity fastballs October typically has to offer.
The Phillies have two superstar sluggers in Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper who can do that. Schwarber and Harper are two of the three best fastball hitters in the game this season.
Highest batting run value vs. fastballs, 2026
- Yordan Alvarez: +32 runs created
- Kyle Schwarber: +30 runs created (27 HR, most in MLB)
- Bryce Harper: +28 runs created (18 HR)
- Willson Contreras: +25 runs created
- Ben Rice: +23 runs created
They can slug velo, too. Against fastballs 97 mph or faster this season, Harper is slugging .523 with three home runs. Schwarber is slugging .525 with six homers, the most of any hitter.
This doesn't change in the playoffs, either. Since their first postseason run together in Philadelphia in 2022, Harper is the best fastball hitter in the playoffs, and Schwarber is fourth, with only Yordan and Juan Soto between them. Harper is slugging .778 with seven homers against fastballs, and Schwarber is slugging .722 with 10 homers.
8) Watch out for the Yankees' fastball varieties
Fastball velocity goes up in October, and the Yankees have some explosive heaters -- led, of course, by Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler, whose 98 mph four-seam fastball is tied for the most valuable pitch in the Majors this year.
But what you're really going to see from the Yankees' playoff rotation -- particularly Schlittler and Max Fried -- is a lot of different fastballs. Schlittler and Fried both throw all three types of fastball: four-seamer, sinker and cutter. That variety even within the same pitch group is going to give them an advantage attacking whatever type of lineup they face in the playoffs, and allow them to change up their pitch mix the more they face hitters in a game or series.
Look at their pitch usage from 2025, for example. Schlittler and Fried both mixed and matched their three fastballs in a more balanced way in the playoffs than they did in the regular season.
Schlittler in 2025
- Reg. season: 56% 4-seamers / 20% cutters / 6% sinkers
- Postseason: 43% 4-seamers / 24% cutters / 22% sinkers
Fried in 2025
- Reg. season: 29% cutters / 18% sinkers / 12% 4-seamers
- Postseason: 22% cutters / 20% sinkers / 12% 4-seamers
9) The Padres' bullpen is loaded
We thought about picking "the Padres have three top-10 hitters since the All-Star break" for this (shoutout Fernando Tatis Jr., Jackson Merrill and Ty France), but bullpens play such an outsized role in October -- and San Diego has an awesome one.
In fact, by Statcast's expected ERA metric, which takes into account a pitcher's quality of contact allowed, strikeouts and walks, the Padres have three top-10 pitchers: Bradgley Rodriguez (10th), Adrian Morejon (seventh) and, of course, Mason Miller (first).
We could really write this whole thing about Miller, who's simply the most dominant reliever on the planet and throws baseball's most unhittable pitch, his slider.
Miller's slider has generated a 56% whiff rate this season, the highest of any qualifying pitch type on Statcast's leaderboard, and racked up a ridiculous 75 strikeouts. It misses bats by almost 10 inches on average, the biggest miss distance of any pitch type in the league.
Oh, and he threw that slider 60% of the time last playoffs. So you know it's coming again this October. You still won't be able to hit it.

Title: Proposed state Health Department rules on infectious diseases shouldn't be partisan punching bag [editorial]
Article_Text:
THE ISSUE
Proposed changes to Pennsylvania Department of Health regulations pertaining to communicable diseases are drawing concerns from Republican lawmakers. The proposed rules, published in the Pennsylvania Bulletin last month, represent the first significant changes since 2001, according to state health officials.
The proposed health regulation changes are a kind of Rorschach test, the psychological test that assesses a person’s personality and emotional characteristics — that is, people see in them what they’re disposed to see.
To Democrats, they are a routine updating of rules due, after 25 years, for revision. As the document published in the Pennsylvania Bulletin explained, the regulations need to be updated to expand the list of “reportable diseases, infections and conditions” and to address new recommendations from experts such as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the American Academy of Pediatrics.
To Republicans, the proposed rules are yet more proof that Democratic officials want to control the health decisions of Pennsylvanians.
The Republican narrative is that power-hungry Democrats used the COVID-19 pandemic to wield control over public health by imposing draconian mask mandates and locking down schools and businesses.
We believe those measures — however clumsily implemented — were necessary to stem the spread of an unfamiliar virus that would end up killing more than a million of our fellow Americans.
But we also believe state health officials failed to be as transparent as possible during the pandemic and are repeating that mistake during the current measles outbreak in Pennsylvania.
So, we somewhat understand the Republican skepticism, but we think it’s verging on hysteria for the sake of scoring political points at a shaky time for the GOP’s electoral prospects.
As with the issue of election integrity, Republicans are ramping up distrust in public health even as they accuse state health officials of causing that distrust.
And they are emotively blaming the administration of former Democratic Gov. Tom Wolf for — in the words of GOP state Sen. Doug Mastriano — the pandemic-era “empty classrooms, canceled proms, graduations and lost sports seasons,” when those closures were necessitated by a deadly virus for which there was not yet a widely available vaccine.
Were the school closures hugely inconvenient and detrimental to student academic success and mental health? Yes. But there weren’t any alternatives at a time when hospitals were packed with people dying of COVID-19, healthcare workers were risking their lives to care for them, and the effects of the virus on children were unknown.
In an LNP | LancasterOnline column published last weekend, state Rep. Bryan Cutler of Drumore Township — the former state House speaker — revisited the political battles over the commonwealth’s pandemic measures and trumpeted the GOP’s success in passing two amendments to the state constitution restricting the governor’s emergency powers.
“Because of these battles,” Cutler wrote, “we believed we had ensured that Pennsylvanians’ freedoms would not be trampled in the name of public health ordinances. Now I believe those safeguards are once again at risk.”
He and other Republicans are taking issue with a proposed rule that would allow public health officials to enter places — including schools and homes — without warrants.
We agree that this sounds alarming. But as state Health Department deputy press secretary Stephanie Nojiri stated in an email to the LNP | LancasterOnline Editorial Board, “The proposed regulations do not create new legal authority for the Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH) to enter private residences or change how the Department respects private property. The proposed regulations clarify the authority that already exists in statute.”
As the proposed rule document states, the Department of Health simply wants to “move requirements pertaining to investigations” from one section to another, “so that all disease control measures are in one place, which will make it easier for the regulated community to find them.”
Under the proposed regulations, a school would need to allow state health officials to meet in private with an employee or student who has been exposed to an infectious disease.
State Rep. Tom Jones of Elizabethtown, who’s running for a Pennsylvania Senate seat, asserted on Facebook that a private meeting with a student “could lead to a student being convinced to take a vaccine or other treatment without notification to the parent or guardian.”
This is extremely unlikely. School and health officials know that this would invite a firestorm.
But there is one reasonable concern that demands the Department of Health’s attention.
As LNP | LancasterOnline reported, Nathan Mains, CEO of the Pennsylvania School Boards Association, wrote to the regulatory commission reviewing the proposed regulations, asserting that they risk “placing school administrators, teachers, nurses, and other personnel in direct conflict with parental expectations by requiring them to facilitate interactions involving highly sensitive health matters while restricting their ability to communicate with families regarding those interactions.”
As Nojiri told an LNP | LancasterOnline news journalist, the proposed regulations do not give the state Department of Health new legal authority to speak to children without parental consent but, instead, provide “transparency” about the agency’s existing work during disease investigations and contact tracing.
Nevertheless, it would seem imperative that the Department of Health clarify what school officials can relate to parents and caregivers.
Cutler and other Republicans are also displeased that Pennsylvania health regulations are being rewritten without legislative input. But the state Health Department has been welcoming comments on the rule change document since Aug. 8 and will continue doing so through Monday.
Pennsylvanians can submit comments on the proposed regulations via email at RA-DHCHAPTR27PROPREG@pa.gov.
We urge people, lawmakers included, to weigh in.
We fear that the state’s handling of COVID-19 will be relitigated again and again, in perpetuity — especially if state health officials keep opening the doors to critics and conspiracy theorists by being unnecessarily secretive about the victims of disease outbreaks, as is happening now with measles.
Four Pennsylvanians — including two infants in Lancaster County — now have succumbed to “measles-associated” deaths. We wish that instead of waging overheated political battles about rule changes, elected officials of all political affiliations were focusing on promoting measles vaccination.
The proposed rule changes are important and if they were being debated in good faith, we would laud the exercise of civic engagement.
But yet again, a matter related to public health is being turned into a political game in which no one wins, least of all ordinary Pennsylvanians.

Title: President Trump abandons the base that's never abandoned him [column] | Local Voices
Article_Text:
One of Donald Trump’s most famous pronouncements occurred Jan. 23, 2016, during his first Republican presidential campaign, when he told supporters at a rally in Iowa: “They say I have the most loyal people — did you ever see that? — where I could stand in the middle of Fifth Avenue and shoot somebody, and I wouldn’t lose any voters.”
It seems as if the president is devoting his second term to finding out whether the proposition is true.
Trump’s record of broken promises is striking when you tally his launch of a costly war in the Middle East, failure to curb inflation and refusal to fully comply with the Epstein Files Transparency Act.
Then there is last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which is ballooning the federal deficit by trillions of dollars, cutting Medicaid and threatening the solvency of Medicare, contrary to the president’s pledges to do none of those things.
Adding insult to injury, some of the president’s actions appear specifically targeted at Republican supporters.
His tariffs are hurting farmers and small businesses. Escalation of the trade war with Canada is inflicting economic pain on Northern states stretching from Alaska to the Dakotas to Pennsylvania.
Likewise, many blue-collar white workers — the core of Trump’s base — have soured on the president, citing high gas prices, slow job growth (especially for men) and the president’s indifference to the affordability issue.
Instead, the president’s priority appears to be remaking the architecture of the nation’s capital.
What’s in a name?
According to a PolitiFact analysis of Trump’s public appearances over the first seven months of 2026, he spoke more about the White House ballroom, Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and proposed triumphal arch than on any other topic except the war against Iran.
His latest obsession is getting his name affixed to the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, which the governing board he controls has shut down amid reports that the institution is on the brink of bankruptcy.
Trump was enraged by a federal court ruling that only Congress can decide the naming question because it was Congress’ decision to memorialize the late John F. Kennedy “and no one else” by naming the center for him. Trump told reporters that without him, the Kennedy Center is “going to close.” He added: “It’ll end up being ripped down.”
Ominously, as The New York Times reported, “Late Wednesday night, photojournalists captured images through the windows of Air Force One that showed President Trump reviewing a large poster board with what looked like a rendering of a construction site beneath three very visible words: ‘Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED.’”
Going full speed ahead
Political observers wonder whether Trump even cares about who wins the midterm elections.
The president waited until this month to open his $400 million campaign war chest. He is unlikely to fund GOP candidates who do not enthusiastically praise his achievements.
Unfortunately for Trump, his brand has become toxic.
Analyzing more than a million social media messages by party politicians in September, The Washington Post found that fewer than 10% of Republican candidates referred to the president by name. And, remarkably, Republican U.S. Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, who represents a red district in south Florida, issued a campaign ad Thursday that denounces Trump’s immigration enforcement efforts as having “gone too far.”
As for artificial intelligence safety — the hottest topic of the fall and maybe many falls thereafter — Trump claimed the issue was a “hoax” and the product of a “sick conspiracy,” even as AI leaders sounded warnings about the technology’s potential excesses.
With polls indicating nearly 70% of the public oppose data centers and are worried about AI, the president’s full-speed-ahead approach is making his party nervous.
Trump knows best
How did we get to the point where a president is punishing his political base rather than rewarding it?
One answer is Trump’s personality, through which the president has convinced himself of his greatness, or, as he posted on his social media platform, that he is “a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT” who knows best in all things.
A second response is the almost total lack of restraint on the president’s worst impulses by family, staff, Cabinet, the Republican Party, Congress or the U.S. Supreme Court.
Another enabler is Trump’s cult following in the public and in conservative media, which forgives his mistakes and blames his enemies for every transgression. It is important to remember that about 35% of Americans continue to support the president through thick and thin.
There is also a larger context. Without political polarization, there would not be a Trump phenomenon.
Through the 1950s, 1960s and 1970s, the conventional wisdom among political scientists and analysts was that national political candidates must run to the center of the political spectrum to win elections.
Prototypical centrists were winning presidential candidates Dwight Eisenhower, John F. Kennedy and Jimmy Carter.
Candidates who went to ideological extremes, such as conservative U.S. Sen. Barry Goldwater in 1964 and liberal U.S. Sen. George McGovern in 1972, lost elections by landslide margins.
Things began to change in the 1980s when Ronald Reagan, the most conservative Republican standard-bearer since Goldwater, won twice handily. However, Reagan was followed into the White House by two classic centrists, George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton.
Base strategy
By the mid-1990s, though, several trends and events coincided to polarize political elites and, in turn, the electorate. Probably the most important changes were deregulation of the broadcast media and the emergence of partisan cable television.
Right-wing sources of political news and information, led by Fox News and the radio provocateur Rush Limbaugh, emerged and dominated the airwaves.
Add to this mix the horrific events of Sept. 11, 2001, which launched the nation into wars in Afghanistan and Iraq under the leadership of President George W. Bush. Bush framed the terrorist attacks in moralistic terms, which broadened into domestic politics on issues such as same-sex marriage.
By the 2004 election, surveys showed that 40% of voters self-identified as conservative, compared to only about 20% identifying as liberal. Moreover, political scientists found that most self-declared independents are really closet partisans.
Buoyed by these findings, Bush’s political strategist, Karl Rove, reasoned that Republicans could win national elections not by moving to the center, but instead by mobilizing the conservative base. Bush won reelection over Democrat John Kerry by a narrow margin.
Rove believed the base strategy could lead Republicans to national political dominance for a generation or more. The Iraq War’s unpopularity, the Great Recession and Barack Obama shattered that dream, but polarization did not subside — in fact, it intensified.
While a GOP study group recommended in 2013 that the party expand its outreach to women, LGBTQ+ groups and people of color, one prospective presidential candidate for 2016 had a different idea.
‘America First’
Running as a political outsider, Donald Trump sought not so much to expand but rather transform the Republican base by appealing to the white working class.
Offending big business interests (except when it came to cutting taxes and government regulations), Trump repudiated orthodox GOP positions favoring free trade and immigration. His “America First” platform championed economic nationalism and condemned intervention in foreign wars.
At the same time, he embraced culture war issues advocated by Christian conservatives, opposing abortion and gay rights and appointing judges vetted by conservative legal groups.
In essence, Trump became a movement leader with a loyal and passionate following that has powered him through three presidential contests despite never achieving 50% or higher approval ratings in Gallup polls.
Vicious, vulgar and self-aggrandizing in public appearances and messaging, the president exacerbated polarization and personalized the base strategy.
Trump’s other contribution to the evolution of 21st-century electoral politics has been a comprehensive attempt to weaken his political opposition.
For example, Democrats believe the proposed strict proof-of-citizenship requirements in the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act and restrictions on mail and early voting would likely disenfranchise more of their voters than Republicans.
Additional demobilization initiatives include the Trump administration’s attempts to gain control of voter rolls, mid-decade gerrymanders by red states, and the U.S. Supreme Court’s gutting of Voting Rights Act protections of minority voters.
And we haven’t even mentioned Trump’s occasional threats to investigate, prosecute or otherwise intimidate Democratic leaders.
Of course, many of the president’s efforts to undermine the opposition party have either not succeeded or been approved by Congress, the courts or the states. For example, the U.S. Supreme Court last Monday blocked the Trump administration’s scheme to implement new Postal Service rules for voting by mail.
The ‘Trump dividend’
As the countdown to Election Day shortens and his standing in the polls drops further, Trump is getting more desperate.
Which brings us back to Trump’s relationship with his increasingly restless supporters.
The only remaining group over which the president can exercise some degree of control — as well as provide him the constant adulation he demands — is the MAGA movement.
At the Republican midterm convention held in Dallas, Texas, earlier this month, Trump promised to give $5,000 checks to all adult Americans if the GOP retains control of the U.S. House and Senate in the Nov. 3 midterms.
Urging his supporters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot,” the president pleaded for them to go to the polls.
Trump led the delegates in a pledge of allegiance to himself, “the greatest president in the history of the United States, that loves us so much he can’t even breathe.”
Ironically, the man who falsely claimed voter fraud cost him reelection in 2020 begged his supporters, whether “registered (to vote) or not,” to “cheat like hell” if necessary.
What if Republicans stay home instead? What if they don’t want the money promised to them by Trump or don’t believe it will ever come?
What if his followers appear ungrateful? Could the president’s love for his people go unrequited?
Donald Trump is not the kind of man who takes rejection well.
Look at the Kennedy Center now — if, that is, it’s still standing when you read this.
E. Fletcher McClellan, Ph.D., is professor of political science emeritus at Elizabethtown College; Bluesky: @mcclelef.bsky.social.

Title: Knife attack on Sikh trucker in Wyoming stirs fresh fears in community
Article_Text:
FORT COLLINS, Colo. — The stabbing of a truck driver at a remote Wyoming rest stop had U.S. Sikhs on edge Friday amid rising anti-immigrant vitriol against the community and its truck drivers in particular.
The Sikh victim was attacked from behind early Sunday while in a restroom at the Bitter Creek rest stop on Interstate 80 midway between Cheyenne and Salt Lake City, according to court documents. He suffered stabs to the neck and chest and over a dozen other cuts but survived.
While police say the motive is unknown, the attack came after deadly crashes involving Sikh truck drivers led to debate about commercial driver’s licensing requirements — sparking hatred toward Sikhs as a group, community leaders said.
Anti-Sikh sentiment has been especially severe on truck-driving forums, said one Sikh in the trucking industry, Harsimran Singh, CEO of Gillson Trucking in Stockton, California.
“I’ve been here for the last 25-plus years,” Singh said. “I never felt this kind of hate before.”
Police were still investigating what prompted the Wyoming attack by a man who left the rest area driving a truck-trailer combination, Sweetwater County Sheriff’s Department spokesperson Jeff Sheaman said.
“We have zero motive,” Sheaman said.
The victim allegedly told police he was trying to use the restroom when he was attacked from behind. He pushed the attacker, he said, and didn’t see the knife at first, according to the police affidavit filed in the case.
Within hours, police arrested Andrew Kris Bzdak in nearby Carbon County, Wyoming. A family at the rest area who heard the attack allegedly followed Bzdak’s truck back onto the highway and tipped off police to help find him, according to the affidavit.
Video taken from a truck at the rest area showed the victim walk casually into the restroom, followed by a man police said was Bzdak. Soon after, Bzdak allegedly was recorded running from the restroom, followed by the stumbling, wounded victim who fell at least once, according to the affidavit.
Bzdak remained jailed on $1 million bond Friday in Rock Springs, on suspicion of attempted murder, a crime punishable in Wyoming by up to life in prison. An initial appearance was scheduled for Thursday.
A phone message left at an address for Bzdak in Catawissa, Pennsylvania, wasn’t immediately returned, nor was a phone message for him at the jail and for his Wyoming public defender, Gary Arnell.
Despite no evident motive, the attack was unnerving for Sikhs, who number around 750,000 in the U.S. Many live in California.
Sikh men wear beards, uncut hair and turbans, and many work as truck drivers. Advocacy groups estimate at least 150,000 Sikh truck drivers work in the U.S.
In August 2025, authorities said a Sikh truck driver’s U-turn on a Florida turnpike caused a crash that killed three people. The crash prompted investigations as well as reports about Sikh truck drivers being harassed.
Then last October, a Sikh truck driver accused of being under the influence of drugs caused a fiery crash that killed three people, authorities said.
Both drivers were in the U.S. illegally, according to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which Singh, the trucking CEO, blamed for stirring anti-immigrant hatred with social media posts.
One such post, since taken down, showed a dark-skinned man with a beard that read, “Get off our roads, you don’t know how to drive Mr. Singh.” DHS officials have said the post referred specifically to the driver in the Florida crash. But Sikh community representatives pointed out that a large number of Sikhs — well over 100,000 in the U.S. and millions worldwide — have the last name Singh.
No matter what motivated the attack, the crime is difficult to separate from racism toward Sikhs, said Jasjit Singh, legal services director for the Sikh community group Jakara Movement and a representative of the victim.
“We were making noise about this,” Jasjit Singh said. “That is how the community feels. Until something really bad happens to us, nothing is going to really happen.”
The victim was headed home Friday after five days in a Casper hospital and hopes to drive his truck across Wyoming again, Jasjit Singh said.
But Harsimran Singh, the trucking CEO, also remained apprehensive.
“We are probably going to see more of this,” Harsimran Singh said. “I’m not surprised that it has happened.”

Title: Trump criticised as 'wretched' after remarks on power to ban fishing
Article_Text:
Trump criticised as ’wretched’ after remarks on power to ban fishing
The U.S. president made the hypothetical comment while discussing executive orders to expand access to hunting and fishing; legal experts said he could not impose a nationwide ban unilaterally
U.S. President Donald Trump faced criticism from some social-media users after joking at a White House Rose Garden dinner on Thursday, 17 September 2026, that he could have banned fishing and describing the power of the presidency as "crazy."
The remarks, directed at Bass Pro Shops founder Johnny Morris, prompted online accusations that Trump was "drunk on power," with one user describing his behaviour as "wretched."
What Trump said at the Rose Garden dinner
The comments came during an event attended by more than 100 hunters, anglers and outdoor-industry representatives. It was held after Trump signed executive orders aimed at expanding access to hunting and fishing on public lands and reversing certain restrictions introduced during the Biden administration.
According to video and transcript material from the event, Trump said the administration's measures would expand fishing seasons and quotas. One executive order directs federal agencies to review, revise, suspend or rescind certain regulations affecting saltwater anglers, boaters, charter operators and coastal communities.
Trump then turned to the potential commercial consequences of a hypothetical fishing ban. "I could have made it so you couldn't sell anything. I could have banned fishing," Trump said, addressing Morris directly. "The power of this office is crazy."
He added that he could have banned fishing and driven "Johnny" "right the hell out of business." Trump then suggested hypothetically that he might issue a short-term order before the businessman pleaded with him to reverse it. "I think I'm gonna do that, maybe just a quick order, maybe just for a day or two, till he calls me and he says, Please, President, please, you're putting me out of business, sir."
In his surrounding remarks, Trump presented the idea as hypothetical before describing a short-term order and returning to the broader discussion of fishing policy.
Social-media reaction and the "wretched" description
The clip quickly became the subject of debate online. One X user, posting under the name Runas Dos Lunas, wrote in a post translated from Spanish: "Trump says, smiling, that he could ban fishing for a couple of days just because the position allows him to. It's not a joke."
The user argued that fishing was connected to trade, food and local livelihoods, rather than being merely a leisure activity. The post concluded by describing the president's apparent casualness as "wretched" and saying, "I feel disgust."
Another user wrote, "For anyone who doesn't know what drunk with power means, this here is a great example." A further commenter asked whether Trump's supporters believed he was the best person available for the presidency.
A third commenter focused on Trump's tone rather than the policy itself, writing that he appeared to be enjoying the idea of telling millions of Americans they could no longer fish. Another accused him of mocking the people who voted for him.
Some users criticised Trump's smile and delivery, interpreting the remarks as boastful rather than as a serious warning.
Why Trump's fishing remarks drew mixed reactions online
Some users did not interpret the fishing remarks as a serious threat. "Don't take him seriously. He's a natural comedian," one commenter wrote. The remarks did not constitute an announcement of a fishing prohibition. The transcript shows Trump discussing an existing policy change before introducing the ban as a hypothetical. The sharp reaction instead centred on whether joking about taking away people's livelihoods was appropriate in the first place.
Trump's wording also raised questions online about the scope of presidential authority, although the statement itself does not establish what legal authority a president would have to impose a nationwide fishing ban. Experts told reporters that the president does not have the power or authority to make such a decision.
"There is no plausible basis on which he could ban fishing throughout the U.S.," said Ilya Somin, an author and law professor at George Mason University. Kate Shaw, a law professor at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School, agreed that there was no legal way for the president simply to ban fishing throughout the U.S., but said what the statement represented could be concerning.
The White House executive order itself says implementation must be consistent with applicable law and preserves authorities granted to executive departments and agencies. Trump said he could have banned fishing, but that is a quotation rather than an established legal power.

Title: This swing state Republican keeps distancing himself from Trump. It may not save him in the midterms
Article_Text:
YARDLEY, Pa. (AP) — Mary Ryan may be a registered Republican but she has never voted for President Donald Trump, turned off by his crass style of politics and chaotic approach to governing.
But the 60-year-old medical writer from the Philadelphia suburbs has consistently backed her party’s congressman, five-term Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick.
Until now.
This year, Ryan is so fed up with Trump and his grip on Congress that she is planning to vote in November for Fitzpatrick’s Democratic opponent in the 1st Congressional District, Bob Harvie, a twice countywide elected commissioner who is a former social studies teacher.
Even though Fitzpatrick has pitched himself as a voice of reason in Washington, Ryan said that “I don’t see it happening.”
Defections like this one could sink Fitzpatrick’s reelection chances and cost Republicans their narrow U.S. House majority. As one of the few Republicans representing a congressional district won by Democrat Kamala Harris in the presidential race two years ago, Fitzpatrick has done as much as any House Republican to distance himself from Trump: Fitzpatrick voted against Trump’s tariffs, his signature tax legislation and his power to wage war against Iran without congressional approval. The lawmaker even skipped Trump’s recent midterm convention in Dallas.
But that may not be enough to overcome the collateral damage of the president’s sagging approval rating and soaring fuel prices because of the war.
Fitzpatrick, speaking briefly after a Sept. 11 memorial in his district, said he understands this year’s political challenges and always considers what is best for his constituents with every vote.
“That’s the job,” he said. Representatives for Fitzpatrick did not respond to requests for a more complete interview.
Democrats have tried for years to defeat Fitzpatrick
Harvie describes the race and his decision to run in almost existential terms.
“The lack of trust in our government, the lack of trust in each other and seeing each other as enemies based just on, you know, the color of your skin, the religion you practice, who you voted for,” he said in an interview this summer. “I worry about just the basic foundations of this nation.”
Fitzpatrick has consistently survived challenges in his politically mixed district. He won by 13 percentage points in 2024 when Harris won by less than a single point in the district. In 2022, he won by about 10 points when Democrats were elected to the U.S. Senate and governorship. In 2020, Democratic presidential nominee Joe Biden won the district by about 5 points while Fitzpatrick carried it by about 13 points.
“Every two years Democrats in Washington label Congressman Fitzpatrick as vulnerable. Every two years he wins anyway,” said Robert Speel, an associate professor of political science at the Penn State campus in Erie. “It’s, to some extent, possibly like Charlie Brown trying to kick the football and failing each time.”
Harvie pointed to his deep roots in the district as a basis for why he could be different from previous Democrats who ran against Fitzpatrick.
“I’m not somebody who needs to be reintroduced or introduced to people of this district. And that’s very, very different than any race he’s ever run before,” he said.
Jean Dolan, 61, is a Democratic voter from Newtown who has never backed Fitzpatrick and does not plan to this year. She has been frustrated with Trump’s immigration crackdown and she worries about how anti-vaccine sentiment in his administration could affect public health. As she sees it, Fitzpatrick is not independent enough from his party’s leaders.
“He’s a nice guy. I know people like him a lot in the community,” she said. But, she added, “you have to serve everyone in your district.”
Fitzpatrick has been willing to criticize Trump
Fitzpatrick graduated with an MBA and a law degree and worked as a special agent for the FBI and as an assistant U.S. attorney. He also worked in private practice as a lawyer and accountant before running for the seat previously held by his brother, Mike Fitzpatrick, who died of cancer in 2020.
Jim Rachau, a 45-year-old photographer from Doylestown, is a registered independent who plans to vote for Fitzpatrick again this year. Rachau is not thrilled with the war or the economy, but said Fitzpatrick has earned his support with his prior public service as an FBI agent.
“You would think serving for the public good, he would have their best interest at heart,” Rachau said.
In Congress, Fitzpatrick has not shied away from disagreeing with Trump. He criticized the president, for example, in April when Trump called Pope Leo XIV “weak,” and captive to the “Radical Left.”
“There’s so many angry voices out there. We all know that’s the case,” Fitzpatrick said in an episode of a podcast launched this year with U.S. Rep. Tom Suozzi, a Democrat who represents a battleground district in New York. “People are sick and tired of the noise. They’re sick and tired of elected officials not being focused on the kitchen table issues that people really care about.”
Fitzpatrick also posts online regularly about meeting with groups across the district. He recently showed up to a picket line with striking sheet metal workers; he dropped by a local Catholic church’s parish picnic; and he stopped at a community college hosting a maternity coalition.
Fitzpatrick spends millions on attack ads against Harvie
Fitzpatrick has also unleashed a wave of spending in the race already, disbursing nearly $5 million, according to Federal Election Commission records.
Negative attack ads against Harvie have mushroomed. Many claim Harvie is under FBI investigation, which the Democrat denies. He has filed a federal defamation lawsuit against a super PAC running some of the ads.
According to the suit, local media reported in 2020 with few details that the FBI was investigating local government and that Harvie was called to testify as a witness in the case. His attorneys say he has never been charged.
The FBI did not respond to a request for comment.
No debate has been scheduled between Fitzpatrick and Harvie, but the men appeared at the same Sept. 11 memorial, standing on opposite sides of the speaker’s lectern. They did not appear to speak to each other.
Ryan, the medical writer from the Philadelphia suburbs, said she is thinking less about Fitzpatrick and more about how Republicans in Congress and their reluctance to buck the president.
“Incumbents just feel they can’t cross that line. If they do, they’re not going to get reelected,” she said. But she acknowledged that may not matter in the end. “They might not get reelected anyway.”

Title: New laws trigger a fresh legal fight over Nazi-looted art in Los Angeles and Auschwitz museums
Article_Text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Jewish heirs of Holocaust victims and their representatives have filed two lawsuits in California staking their claims to Nazi-looted paintings that still hang on the walls of prominent museums in Los Angeles and Auschwitz.
This pair of lawsuits are the first to be filed after the recent passage of laws by California and Congress, which strengthen U.S.-based claims to artwork that were forcibly taken from Jewish families during World War II.
One lawsuit was filed in Los Angeles Superior Court on Monday by the Jewish Federation of Greater Los Angeles and its board chair Daniel Gryczman against Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena for the return of “Adam and Eve.” These are two life-size oil-on-panel masterpieces created by Lucas Carnach the Elder in 1530.
The other lawsuit was filed in federal court in Los Angeles the same day by the daughters of the late Dinah Gottliebova Babbitt, a Holocaust survivor and California-based animator who was held in Auschwitz. It demanded the return of watercolors of fellow prisoners that the artist was forced to paint for Josef Mengele, a Nazi physician who had earned the nickname the “Angel of Death.”
Spokespersons for both museums say the museums legally hold titles to the works, and intend to continue displaying them to the public. The lawsuits don’t specify the monetary value of the paintings.
Artworks pit Jewish families against museums
The issue of Nazi-looted art is an emotional, legally and ethically charged topic that pits Jewish families that have suffered inter-generational trauma against museums that say they are trying to preserve a painful, yet important, chapter of history. Between 1933 and 1945, the Nazi regime orchestrated the largest art theft in world history, seizing over 600,000 works of art across Europe from Jewish families, collectors and museums. Decades later, many of these masterpieces reside in prominent museums around the world, making the push for their recovery more complex than a simple property dispute.
Rabbi Noah Farkas is president and CEO of the Jewish Federation of Los Angeles, the organization to which Marei von Saher, sole heir of Dutch Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker, has signed over her rights. The paintings were seized from Goudstikker’s collection by Hermann Goring, Adolf Hitler’s second-in-command and changed a number of hands before being sold in the 1960s to the Pasadena Museum of Modern Art, which was renamed Norton Simon Museum in honor of its benefactor.
Farkas said the federation plans to use most of the net proceeds from the recovered art to provide much-needed help to the about 2,500 Holocaust survivors living in the Los Angeles area.
“These are incredibly beautiful European masterpieces stolen from a Jewish family to enrich the Nazi party and fund the war and death machine against the people,” he said. “It’s our honor to take on this role on behalf of the community and use most of the proceeds to help these elderly survivors live out the last years of their lives in dignity, comfort and peace – something their family members were denied during the Holocaust.”
Marei von Saher, in a statement, said she is grateful to the Jewish organization for taking up her family’s cause.
“This effort represents a meaningful step toward justice for Holocaust survivors and victims of Nazi era atrocities,” she said.
New legislation gives lawsuits second wind
California Assemblyman Jesse Gabriel, D-Woodland Hills, wrote Assembly Bill 2867, signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom in September 2024, which requires that the state law must apply in lawsuits brought by California residents or their heirs to recover art seized during the Holocaust or during other acts of persecution. Gabriel, who co-chairs the California Legislative Jewish Caucus, introduced the legislation in response to a federal court ruling, which allowed the state-owned Thyssen-Bornemisza National Museum in Madrid to keep a multimillion-dollar Camille Pissarro impressionist masterpiece.
That painting had been taken by the Nazis from the Cassirer family in 1939. This case, which prompted this new law, is expected to be heard in federal court in California next month.
Gabriel said it’s time for museums to “do some deep introspection on whether they want to be on the right side of history.”
Museums want to preserve paintings for posterity
Norton Simon Museum released a statement pointing out that a federal court in 2018 unanimously determined that the museum had proper title to the Cranach paintings. In May 2019, the U.S. Supreme Court declined to get involved in the case, leaving in place lower court rulings.
They said the Cranach paintings, which originally belonged to the Stroganoff family, were put up for sale in 1931 by the Soviet Union in an illicit auction in Berlin where they were purchased by Goudstikker. After a complicated journey, the paintings were sold to the museum by a Stroganoff family descendant. The museum later restored and preserved the pieces.
“For nearly 50 years, they have been on view at the Norton Simon Museum and will continue to be accessible to the public for years to come,” the statement said.
Pawel Sawicki, a spokesperson for the Auschwitz Memorial, said the watercolors of Roma victims that Gottliebova Babbitt was forced to paint by Mengele to document his horrendous experiments and racial research, “must remain in the Memorial” to document the man’s crimes. He said these paintings must not be mischaracterized as “Nazi-looted art” because Gottliebova Babbitt painted them against her will as a prisoner and therefore didn’t have ownership of the watercolors.
While he understands the family’s sentiments, Sawicki said the portraits of Roma and Sinti victims are among the few remaining documents of Mengele’s criminal experiments and should be treated as unique documents related to the history of the Auschwitz concentration camp.
“While fully respecting the rights of people who created some of the documents here, we are of the opinion that any loss in the collections of the Memorial will constitute irreparable harm,” he said. “ … The loss of even the smallest part of the documentation is an irreparable loss and blemish on the memory of the victims of Auschwitz.”
Advocates hope cases will now be heard on their merit
Joel Greenberg, founder of Art Ashes, a Philadelphia-area nonprofit that helps Jewish families track down and recover Nazi-looted art, said in addition to the California law, President Donald Trump signed into law and updated the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2025. This new law permanently eliminated the expiration date to allow Holocaust survivors and their heirs to indefinitely pursue the recovery of these works of art.
Greenberg said the new federal law gave families the right to reclaim their art for up to six years from the time they find out in whose possession they are.
“These new laws mean that technical defenses will no longer stick in court,” he said. “Every case will be heard on its merits.”
He said the new legislation also ensures that these Jewish families have their day in court and a fair process to determine ownership of the stolen art.
“It will make sure the stories of what happened to European Jewry is not lost and forgotten,” he said. “The art can still be returned to the rightful owner.”

Title: Opinion: Saucon Valley anti-vaping law is the wrong approach
Article_Text:
I was 16 when I started smoking cigarettes. I played keyboards in a bohemian indie band that ended up opening for artists such as Red Hot Chili Peppers and Alex Chilton, and my idols in the music and literature all smoked. I thought it made you sophisticated. I was stupid.
I did not understand nicotine’s addictiveness. Still, as I was finishing high school, I wasn’t hooked enough to risk “smokin’ in the boys room” with the burnouts. By the end of college, I smoked a pack day. I was so impoverished and addicted at one point, I would harvest butts around campus ashtrays and roll my own “snipes.”
I couldn’t break the habit until 2000, at age 34, and it took another five years of nicotine gum before I finally stopped that.
Had I been criminally penalized at 16, it would have made zero difference to my smoking habit. But I know I would have been filled with shame and self-loathing and anger — three emotions many teenagers already possess in abundance.
This week, the Saucon Valley School Board I serve on voted almost unanimously to endow principals and main administrators with the power to hand out tickets to our students caught smoking — nearly all of whom are obviously children.
Only fellow school director Christian Tatu and I voted against this regressive measure (one school director, Donald Carpenter, was not at the meeting). I can’t speak for those who supported the idea at the meeting, and I won’t speculate, but it’s doomed to hurt our district academically and accomplish nothing positive in terms of public health. It’s a wrongheaded approach to helping children kick the habit.
It was 1996 when Gov. Tom Ridge signed a law that formally criminalized smoking by pupils on school property. In 2019, Gov. Tom Wolf expanded the concept to cover vaping.
Seemingly aware of its own wrongheadedness, the statute contains a host of superficially sensible limits meant to soften the impact of a citation — but the fact is, we’re introducing young students to the criminal justice system at a profoundly sensitive moment in their lives.
And for what? According to the Pennsylvania Alliance to Control Tobacco, so-called PUP Laws (“purchase, use and possession”) simply don’t work. They take time, taxpayer resources, and there is no evidence they deter tobacco use. Some states such as Michigan have seen efforts to repeal these laws because, advocates say, they drive tobacco use underground and nurture fear and shame.
As one advocacy organization, Pennsylvania Alliance to Control Tobacco, puts it: “Criminalizing youth for using tobacco products is ineffective, inequitable, and counterproductive to public health.” It also normalizes the idea of schools as annexes of law enforcement.
The smoking citations under the law aren’t supposed to result in a criminal record, and the fines are low, but the stigma of facing a district judge won’t end after the gavel is struck. A teenager will wear the experience like a badge of honor, a scarlet letter — or both.
I knew the stoners who smoked in the boys room or behind the bleachers in high school. They wore Army surplus jackets, ate free lunches, smoked reefer after school and often seemed to come from big families that were poor or marginalized.
In my era, the ’80s, they might have had a much older brother killed in Vietnam, or an alcoholic or abusive parent at home. A few of them were intellectually gifted and found a way out, but the fragile lives of those bathroom smokers and tokers needed counseling and guidance and attention — not fines and reputations as petty criminals.
These tickets in my community’s schools will also force at least one highly paid member of our school administration to spend time in court when the kid shows up to district court with their parents. What a dumb waste. Personally, I want our school officials nurturing academic excellence, not frittering away time in court over teenage vaping melodramas.
No one is minimizing the impact of tobacco use among children. As a former smoker, I deeply regret my years of lighting up. The damage caused by tobacco use in children is astonishing. But the way to prevent smoking and vaping is through education, and isn’t that, after all, what we’re supposed to be doing in our school buildings?
This is a contributed opinion column. Bill Broun of Hellertown teaches at East Stroudsburg University and is a Saucon Valley School District director.
